answer:
Both columns can have current, freshly analyzed statistics and the query can still be badly costed, because per-column statistics are marginals: they describe each column separately, not how values co-occur. The planner combines predicates by multiplying separate selectivities, assuming independence. When the columns are correlated that product is wrong, and every cost derived from the row estimate - scan choice, join order, join algorithm - inherits the error. The book's synthetic case: one location has 90% of devices tagged "portable" while other locations rarely use the tag, so a combined location-and-tag predicate is underestimated.

New extended statistics change the plan only after the object exists and is populated. Creating the extended-statistics object over the column combination is necessary but not sufficient: it gathers no representative sample until ANALYZE runs. Only then does the planner have joint-distribution evidence (functional dependencies, multivariate n-distinct or MCV lists, where the predicate form is supported), and only a newly planned query can use it - re-run EXPLAIN with representative parameters and verify under a controlled workload.

Boundaries: extended statistics do not cover every predicate form; growth, skew and schema changes can invalidate samples; planner cost units are not latency. A cached plan must also be re-planned, which is inference beyond the book's text. Confidence: high on mechanism, medium on the replan boundary.

evidence.claim: Per-column statistics do not encode co-occurrence; correlated predicates defeat the independence assumption and yield bad join or scan estimates.
evidence.note: Observed: 'Correlated predicates can fool naive independence assumptions, producing badly estimated joins or scan plans.'

evidence.claim: A synthetic location-and-tag predicate is underestimated when tag prevalence depends on location.
evidence.note: Observed: 'one location has 90% of devices tagged as portable, while other locations rarely use the tag'; a planner relying on approximate independent selectivities 'may underestimate rows for a combined location-and-tag predicate.'

evidence.claim: Creating an extended-statistics object gathers no representative sample by itself.
evidence.note: Observed: 'creating extended statistics does not itself gather representative samples until ANALYZE runs.'

evidence.claim: Extended statistics plus ANALYZE may improve estimates, but still require an actual EXPLAIN and controlled workload test.
evidence.note: Observed: 'A suitable extended-statistics object ... and ANALYZE may improve estimates; the design still requires an actual EXPLAIN and controlled workload test.'

evidence.claim: Data growth, skew and schema changes can invalidate prior statistical assumptions.
evidence.note: Observed: 'Samples, data growth, skew and schema changes can invalidate prior assumptions.'

evidence.claim: Plans are generated from fresh table statistics and checked by comparing estimated with actual rows; cost units are not elapsed time.
evidence.note: Observed: flow 'Fresh relevant table statistics -> EXPLAIN candidate plan -> Controlled EXPLAIN ANALYZE'; 'estimated cost is in planner units; it should not be read as elapsed milliseconds.'

evidence.claim: Under tenant skew with correlated state values, stored statistics are a plausible cause of incorrect row estimates.
evidence.note: Observed: 'Later one tenant holds 60% of rows and most records are closed'; table row 'Stale histogram or correlation stats | A plausible cause of incorrect row estimates'.

evidence.claim: An existing or cached plan must be regenerated after ANALYZE before new extended statistics can affect execution.
evidence.note: Inference: the book shows statistics feeding plan generation but does not state plan-cache invalidation; treat as mechanism inference, not a measured claim.
